articles.title: Sudan: Vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks in Darfur - Findings from MSF-supported Health Facilities (January 2024- April 2026)
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Routine immunisation must be restored in Darfur El-Geneina – During a period of just over two years during the ongoing war in Sudan, teams from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) across Darfur treated close to 30,000 patients with vaccine-preventable diseases, according to MSF's latest report, Vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks in Darfur. Measles was the most common disease treated, and it mainly affected unvaccinated children. MSF urges the Sudanese health and political authorities to lift barriers and administrative blockages currently preventing vaccines from entering Darfur. We also urge donor countries and the UN to increase funding and provide the vaccines to health authorities. Without immediate action to restore immunisation activities in the country, outbreaks will continue to spiral, and people will keep dying from diseases we have the tools to prevent. Between January 2024 and April 2026, MSF-supported facilities in four states of Darfur, a vast region in western Sudan, recorded more than 28,000 measles cases and nearly 2,000 pertussis (whooping cough) cases. 75 per cent of the patients treated for measles were not vaccinated, and 69 per cent were children under five years old. "Several localities including Tawila, El-Geneina, Rokero, Zalingei, Nyala, and East Jebel Marra saw recurrent transmission over consecutive years, suggesting outbreaks were not fully contained and that immunity gaps persisted despite repeated outbreak response activities,” says Sebastián Traficante, MSF emergency coordinator in Darfur. “Our teams are constantly treating children for diseases that could have been prevented with a vaccine. Many children reach our facilities in critical condition, and they simply don't make it out of the hospital." Wartime collapse of the health system, supply and staffing issues According to the MSF report, the transmission was particularly high in South Darfur, where 10,600 suspected measles cases were reported in the first four months of 2026 alone, exceeding the total number of cases in 2025. Vaccine-preventable diseases are especially dangerous when paired with complications of other medical conditions, such as malaria and malnutrition, which are rampant across Darfur. With the war in its fourth year, Sudan faces one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. In 2026, 34 million people need humanitarian aid and 21 million people cannot get basic or life-saving medical care due to the collapse of the Sudanese health system. According to the World Health Organization, 37 per cent of health facilities across the country are non-functional.1 Those still open in Darfur report severe shortages of staff, medicines, vaccines, equipment and supplies, and many have only partially functioning or non-functioning cold chains to keep vaccines viable. “Routine vaccination services struggle to reach people, especially in remote areas. The supply, transport and storage of vaccines face significant barriers, mostly due to administrative delays, such as in obtaining import approvals and travel permits,” says Dr. Saiful Islam, MSF emergency medical coordinator for South Darfur. “State-level vaccination offices are often not functioning, leaving little monitoring or supervision. Many health facilities have no permanent vaccination staff and rely on volunteers.” Both availability and access are major concerns for communities. In South Darfur, where the burden of vaccine-preventable diseases is highest, only a fraction of facilities has fully functional cold-chain capacities. In Central Darfur, which experienced recent measles and pertussis outbreaks, MSF teams reported that delays in vaccine arrival, administrative approvals and vaccine mobilisation significantly slowed outbreak response activities. Fauzia, mother of three-year-old Faiz “My child had never been vaccinated because we live in a farmland area, about three hours away from Sortony town... Many children in my area are affected by vaccine-preventable diseases.” MSF doctor Algadi visits three-year-old Faiz and his mother Fauzia in the isolation ward of Rokero hospital, in Jabel Marra region. Faiz is suspected to have pertussis (whooping cough). Central Darfur, Sudan, October 2026.© Maxime Le Lijour/MSF When services do not reach communities, families have to travel to find them. But the war has destroyed livelihoods and sent prices skyrocketing, leaving little income for families. For many parents, even the cost of transport to the nearest health facility is out of reach. “My child had never been vaccinated because we live in a farmland area, about three hours away from Sortony town," says Fauzia, the mother of three-year-old Faiz. "The rainy season also makes it complicated to move around. Many children in my area are affected by vaccine-preventable diseases.” Faiz was admitted to Rokero hospital, in Central Darfur, for suspected pertussis. After being examined, the MSF medical team confirmed that he was also affected by meningitis and tetanus. After 16 days in the isolation ward, Faiz passed away. Emergency vaccination campaigns are not enough Disease surveillance is also a major gap. With limited monitoring and follow-up, outbreaks often go undetected until the disease has spread widely, and emergency vaccination campaigns begin too late. Some emergency campaigns have taken place in various parts of Darfur since 2024 and can help contain outbreaks. But these campaigns need to be more efficient, ideally including antigens for several diseases, and they cannot replace routine immunisation. For instance, in Tawila, North Darfur, a severe measles outbreak saw more than 1,900 cases treated at Tawila hospital between January and April 2026. Following an emergency mass vaccination campaign reaching 130,000 children across Tawila town and displacement camps, community transmission was brought to a halt, with cases dropping to just 96 between April and September 2026, a 95 per cent reduction. While targeted emergency campaigns save lives in real time, and we have seen cases drop afterwards, outbreaks of measles, pertussis and other preventable diseases will keep returning across Darfur without a sustained investment in routine vaccination, cold-chain infrastructure, vaccination staff and disease surveillance. "Immunisation in Darfur and the rest of Sudan must be adapted to the reality of the conflict," says Traficante, MSF emergency coordinator. "That means mobile, outreach and catch-up services run by professional vaccination teams. They can reach unvaccinated children where they are, and also act as our eyes in communities, tracking immunisation rates and detecting outbreaks early." MSF calls on health authorities, donors and UN agencies to fund and facilitate mobile and catch-up vaccination across Darfur and the rest of Sudan. MSF also urges all warring parties and authorities in Sudan to immediately remove administrative barriers to the import and transport of vaccines. WHO: https://www.who.int/news/item/14-04-2026-after-three-years-of-conflict--sudan-faces-a-deeper-health-crisis
